books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Progressivism and Woodrow Wilson
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9: Woodrow Wilson won in 1912 on his New Freedom program. In 1913 he cut tariffs with the Underwood Tariff Act and signed the Federal Reserve Act, creating a central banking system of twelve regional banks to steady credit and the currency. The Sixteenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, let Congress collect an income tax. In 1914 the Clayton Antitrust Act outlawed price discrimination and exempted labor unions from antitrust prosecution, and the Federal Trade Commission Act created a commission to police unfair business practices.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Wilson's New Freedom differed from Roosevelt's New Nationalism mainly in that Wilson

options.text: opposed all reform and wanted no change
options.misconception: Wilson signed the Federal Reserve, Clayton, and trade commission acts; he was a reformer, not an opponent of reform.

options.text: wanted to break up monopolies and restore competition
wanted stronger federal regulation of trusts and monopolies
options.misconception: Stronger federal regulation of big business was Roosevelt's New Nationalism, not Wilson's New Freedom.

options.text: supported laissez-faire economics and limited government
options.misconception: Wilson expanded federal power over banking and business; laissez-faire was the old idea both men rejected.

rationales.A: Wilson passed the era's biggest reforms. Opposing reform would leave the Federal Reserve and Clayton Acts unexplained.
rationales.B: Roosevelt accepted big business and wanted government to regulate it; Wilson was more hostile to bigness itself and wanted to break monopolies apart and restore competition. The passage shows him doing it: the Clayton Act and the trade commission.
rationales.C: Regulating big business from above was Roosevelt's approach. Wilson's approach was to break monopolies up.
rationales.D: Wilson built new federal power over banks and business. Laissez-faire would have meant building nothing.
rationales.general:
1. Name Roosevelt's side. New Nationalism accepted large companies and regulated them as a referee would.
2. Name Wilson's side. New Freedom distrusted bigness and aimed to break monopolies up and restore competition.
3. Check the record. Wilson's Clayton Act and trade commission fit the breakup-and-compete approach.
Remember: two reformers can share a goal and split on method, so compare what each one does to big business.
